source_text: Iam videamus illud excellentissimum acumen tuum, quo vidisti quemadmodum refelleres quod a me dictum est, "dimitti concupiscentiam carnis in Baptismo, non ut non sit, sed ut in peccatum non imputetur; quamvis autem reatu suo iam soluto, manet tamen" [n148] . Adversus haec mea verba sic argumentaris homo acutissimus, tamquam ipsam concupiscentiam dixerim per Baptismum reatu liberari; quoniam dixi, "reatu suo iam soluto": velut "suo" dixerim, quo ipsa rea est, eoque soluto illa permaneat absoluta. … Sed hoc tibi potius qui eam bonam praedicas, convenit dicere, "ut bono eius naturali", sicut de infantibus dicitis: "bonum sanctificationis accedat", et sit carnis concupiscentia sancta Dei filia.
pass_a_gloss: Now let us see that most excellent sharpness of yours, by which you saw how you might refute what was said by me, 'the concupiscence of the flesh to be remitted in Baptism, not so that it is not, but so that it is not imputed into sin; although, its guilt already loosed, it nevertheless remains'. Against these my words you so argue, most acute man, as if I had said concupiscence itself through Baptism to be freed from guilt; since I said 'its guilt already loosed': as if I had said 'its' (meaning that) by which it itself is guilty, and that loosed, it remains absolved. But this rather befits you, who preach it good, to say, 'that to its natural good', as you (plural) say of infants, 'the good of sanctification is added', and let the concupiscence of the flesh be a holy daughter of God.
pass_b_english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “Now let us look at that most excellent sharpness of yours, by which you saw how to refute what I said: ‘that the desire of the flesh is forgiven in baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it is not counted as sin; and although its guilt has already been loosed, it still remains.’ Against these words of mine you argue, most acute man, as though I had said that desire itself is freed from guilt through baptism, because I said ‘its guilt having already been loosed’: as though by ‘its’ I meant the guilt by which desire itself is guilty, so that, with that loosed, it remains acquitted.”

“But it suits you rather, since you proclaim it good, to say ‘that to its natural good,’ as you say of infants, ‘the good of sanctification is added,’ and let the desire of the flesh be a holy daughter of God.”

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Keep the rite-name; Julian says praise of baptism is being used to smuggle natural evil.

choices.choice: 2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-d): the old English summarised Augustine's report ('Augustine reports that Julian ...') instead of translating it. Now a translation of the Latin clause(s) that carry Julian's words or Augustine's report of them, with Augustine named as speaker where the words are his; nothing added that the Latin does not say. Omitted stretches inside a paragraph are marked with an ellipsis.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded. This row is Augustine's report; Pass A glosses only the Julian words recoverable here. This row translates Augustine's report addressed to Julian, with Augustine named as speaker; Julian's words are the quoted parts.
